entry.title: Silent coverage failures in rare-event searches and a degeneracy index that predicts them

link.title: Silent coverage failures in rare-event searches and a degeneracy index that predicts them

entry.content: Searches for new physics in low-background experiments infer a non-negative signal strength from few events and often report an upper limit. Nominal frequentist coverage requires both a valid interval construction and an adequate data model. We study how controlled model departures affect lower- and upper-endpoint coverage for six interval procedures in an exact Poisson counting experiment, dark-matter recoil spectra, and a neutrinoless-double-beta-decay peak search. We introduce the Poisson–Fisher degeneracy index $\mathcal I_{\mathrm{PF}}(\delta\nu;\vartheta_0)=(\beta,\gamma)$, which maps a specified expected-count deformation, after projection onto the complete fitted tangent space, to $\beta$, the signed fitted signal shift in profiled standard-error units, and $\gamma$, the Poisson–Fisher norm of the unabsorbed residual. Locally, the sign of $\beta$ identifies the threatened endpoint, while larger $\gamma$ implies greater detectability by the saturated-Poisson goodness-of-fit test used here at a fixed $5\%$ type-I error rate. Across the studied deformations, positive signal-like bias degrades discovery-side coverage while making upper limits conservative; negative signal bias from overestimated signal efficiency can make the upper endpoint undercover. Calibration under the nominal simulator does not protect against misspecification of that simulator relative to the data-generating process. A plausible deformation with large $ \beta $ and small $\gamma$ may therefore evade diagnosis and should be represented by a nuisance constrained with auxiliary information or included in a defensible envelope. In the exactly collinear constrained-nuisance benchmark, modelling the deformation restores coverage at the evaluated grid points, at a quantifiable cost in interval sensitivity.

entry.title: Conditional validity of prediction-powered inference for spatially dependent finite populations

link.title: Conditional validity of prediction-powered inference for spatially dependent finite populations

entry.content: Prediction-powered inference (PPI) combines full-frame predictions with a small labelled sample to estimate finite-population regression coefficients. We establish conditions for the conditional validity of existing calibrated residual-regression PPI estimators under nonuniform label acquisition and spatially dependent prediction errors. Approximate calibration can leave a population-specific displacement: the projection of prediction errors onto coefficient-specific calibration defects. We characterize its role in conditional inference through the noncentrality of a fixed-candidate Wald region. The relevant target-weight function is the coefficient loading divided by acquisition intensity. When mean-approximation error does not dominate, directional covariance control yields a wider sufficient recovery regime than a total residual-energy bound. A bounded spectral-basis theorem gives conditional coverage under directional covariance, tail and nondegeneracy conditions, with Gaussian and bounded non-Gaussian spatial examples. The analysis accounts for estimation of the one-step augmentation and permits same-label selection from a fixed finite library with a common first-order influence vector. A periodic Fourier construction attains the stochastic directional-gap order within a restricted dictionary class. Constructed and real-record-set experiments illustrate why mean calibration need not protect a slope. The results concern descriptive census projection coefficients under the stated sampling and field conditions.

entry.title: Plausible but Not Valid: A Psychometric Audit of LLMs as Synthetic Survey Respondents

link.title: Plausible but Not Valid: A Psychometric Audit of LLMs as Synthetic Survey Respondents

entry.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as synthetic survey respondents, but existing evaluations mostly ask whether individual answers look plausible. We ask a stricter, psychometric question: do LLMs preserve the joint distribution, latent structure, reliability, mediation pathways, and demographic effects of real human survey data? We introduce an open Lithuanian organisational-psychology dataset (n=263 employees; three validated instruments; 68 items, 12 subscales) and condition 37 LLMs on real respondent profiles under a persona-disclosure ladder, presentation, reasoning-effort and cross-language ablations, counterfactual demographic swaps, and a memorization probe. The resulting Psychometric Similarity Score (PSS) is anchored against five statistical baselines, a held-out human ceiling, and the real answers of the same respondents. LLMs reproduce the direction of human psychometric relationships, but statistical baselines with no language model match or beat them. The best LLM (PSS 0.81) is level with a Gaussian copula fit only on other respondents (0.82) and below the real answers of the same 100 people (0.89). A simple classifier separates every LLM sample from humans (median AUC 0.99), and verbatim recall of the items is rare (at most 4.7%) and unrelated to PSS. Counterfactual swaps move answers in the direction of human group differences and by a similar amount (role 0.49 and education 0.33 human SD, vs. 0.46 and 0.44 in humans). Gender swaps move them by 0.06 SD. Tucker’s phi on UWES falls inside an item-permutation null for 10 of 37 models. Synthetic respondents compress the response scale (within-respondent SD 0.79 vs. 1.19), lose predictive validity on held-out humans (mean R^2=-0.14 vs. 0.28), and produce significant indirect effects on 4 of 7 mediation paths that are null in humans. LLM samples are therefore not a drop-in replacement for human survey data.

link.title: Kernelized Stein Discrepancy for Goodness-of-Fit Tests and Stein Sampling in R

entry.content: Stein’s method constructs computable discrepancies between a target distribution and a candidate distribution without requiring the target distribution’s normalizing constant. These discrepancies support goodness-of-fit tests for model assessment as well as sampling tools for empirical approximation. The R package steinsampling provides the first unified R workflow for applying score-based Stein methods to kernel goodness-of-fit testing of independent or serially dependent observations, point transport, greedy point construction, and sample compression. High-level functions carry out each task in a single call, while the kernel, calibration, optimization, and transition components are provided separately so that users can replace any one of them. A single score and kernel setup can therefore be reused across sampling and testing, making these methods easier to reproduce, compare, and extend.

entry.title: Model-assisted estimation with a training subsample: a two-phase sampling approach with design-based variance estimation

link.title: Model-assisted estimation with a training subsample: a two-phase sampling approach with design-based variance estimation

entry.content: When a flexible prediction model is fitted on a training subsample drawn from a probability sample, the model-assisted estimator actually reported arises from one realized partition, yet existing theory quantifies uncertainty only for partition-averaged, cross-fitted, or symmetrized versions of it. We represent the training subsample as a second phase of sampling and derive, exactly and for any algorithm, a two-term variance decomposition and the variance family linking the single-partition estimator to its Rao-Blackwellized average, whose design bias it shares. For cell-mean rules under equal-probability designs the estimator is, exactly, a convex combination of a poststratified plug-in at the training-sample size and the exactly unbiased single-split estimator of Sanguiao Sande and Zhang, which locates its bias precisely. For tree-type predictors the second-phase variance is computable in closed form when the cell structure is fixed or $s$-measurable, and in that regime, for cell counts $H=o(n)$, its share of total variance grows with the number of cells – a design-based mechanism distinct from residual shrinkage and consistent with the variance underestimation documented for flexible learners. We propose an analytic and a replication variance estimator, neither altering the point estimate, and evaluate them by simulation under simple random and stratified designs, in the adaptive regime and in an $s$-measurable configuration in which the theory is exact: in the populations studied, budgeting the second phase recovers much of the coverage lost by ignoring it, and the residual shortfall is attributable to the bias of the point estimator rather than to its variance.

entry.title: Dangers of Bayesian analyses and how to address them

link.title: Dangers of Bayesian analyses and how to address them

entry.content: In light of the US FDA announcement supporting the use of Bayesian methods in clinical trials, we present a nontechnical review of problems with Bayesian analyses and methods to address them. Our focus is on the well-known sensitivities of Bayesian results to biases embedded in their prior distributions. This vulnerability calls for special safety features, including detailed justification of informative priors based on empirical-research literature rather than on singular expert opinions. Crucially, the information contributed by priors should be realistic in light of actual background data rather than merely judged so by available experts. We illustrate our recommendations with using a textbook clinical-trial example which covered these points. We then use the example describe basic diagnostic procedures and safety recommendations for Bayesian analyses and their presentation. These include reference analyses which exclude informative priors, and justification for informative priors based on empirical-research literature rather than on philosophical arguments. We also critique some common priors that violate our realism requirements. One strategy to aid judgments about priors is to translate them into data to be added to the study data. The source of these prior data should be examined with the same critical attitude as the source of study data. We illustrate some simple summary methods for comparing prior and data information, including prior predictions of data, variance ratios, and their translation to effective sample sizes (ESS). Finally, we argue that Bayesian analyses should be treated as extensions or supplements to conventional analyses, rather than replace them, for that treatment puts prior construction and justification at the fore of the transition from frequentist to Bayesian analyses in teaching and practice.

entry.title: Identification and Inference in proxy-SVARs with non-Gaussian shocks

link.title: Identification and Inference in proxy-SVARs with non-Gaussian shocks

entry.content: Two frequent approaches for identifying structural VARs are external instruments, which carry economic content but are often weak, and non-Gaussianity of the shocks, which provides statistical identification but carries no economic meaning. We combine the two strategies in a single generalized method of moments framework. This hybrid approach point-identifies the target shocks while also identifying the non-target shocks up to sign and ordering. Under suitable rank conditions, the higher-order moments of the structural shocks anchor the identification uniformly over the instrument strength. Consequently, under local-to-zero proxy relevance, estimators of the dynamic causal effects remain consistent, and standard asymptotic inference remains valid. Moreover, the Anderson-Rubin confidence sets are substantially narrower than their instrument-only counterparts. The hybrid estimator is also more efficient than either source of identification used in isolation: at any fixed proxy relevance, even a weak instrument increases the efficiency of the estimator through its covariance with the non-Gaussian moment block. Under local deviations from proxy exogeneity, we provide asymptotic bias bounds and show that stronger non-Gaussianity of the shocks compresses the bias. Finally, the over-identified structure yields two mutually orthogonal specification tests for proxy exogeneity and the validity of the higher-order moment conditions. We derive their limiting distributions and provide a bootstrap procedure for finite-sample critical values. Monte Carlo simulations and two applications with identification of oil news-shock and a Euro-area MP shock demonstrate the potential of our framework.

entry.title: Compression Hurts, Pooling Helps: Information Loss in Rayleigh-Scale Estimation from B-Mode Ultrasound

link.title: Compression Hurts, Pooling Helps: Information Loss in Rayleigh-Scale Estimation from B-Mode Ultrasound

entry.content: Clinical B-mode images are widely available as potential data sources for quantitative ultrasound (QUS) analysis for tissue characterization. However, standard clinical ultrasound devices apply unknown log-compression to RF envelope data before display and storage. Previous work has demonstrated estimation of the underlying RF envelope statistics in the presence of an unknown compression law. Using Fisher information analysis, we show that finite-offset log compression causes severe information loss when estimating the Rayleigh scale $\sigma$, which controls diffuse speckle. For a single image window, unknown compression raises the minimum achievable variance for unbiased estimation of $\sigma$ by a compression-independent factor of approximately 34.98. When $M$ equal-sized windows share the same unknown compression settings, the excess variance decays as $1/M$; even in the most favorable regime, reducing the variance inflation factor below 1.1 requires 340 windows. Our analysis treats the contrast parameter $a$ as unknown and the boundary offset $b$ as known; estimating $b$ experimentally shows even larger variance. We validate this theory using synthetic estimation experiments and demonstrate RF-scale recovery on real RF-envelope windows from the OASBUD dataset. Together, these results clarify the limitations of using routine B-mode images for QUS.

entry.title: Federated multiple testing with quantized p-values under family-wise error control

link.title: Federated multiple testing with quantized p-values under family-wise error control

entry.content: Several institutions test one family of hypotheses under family-wise error control but cannot pool their data, so each site releases only a quantized report of its p-value for each hypothesis, such as whether the p-value is significant. The report’s resolution is the number of values it can take. We quantify the power lost to such reports relative to the most powerful centralized procedure given all p-values (the oracle), with reports and combining rule chosen optimally. A report from which the p-value can be recovered loses no power, so the loss is due to compression, not decentralization. Under the stated regularity and power-objective conditions, every finite resolution loses power, and the optimal loss decays as the inverse square of the resolution: equal-width intervals attain this order, and no partition into as many cells improves it. In two-site Beta examples, optimized one-bit reports are nearly lossless for a single hypothesis but lose several times as much power for two. At level 0.05 with two Beta(1,2) hypotheses, optimally combined three-bit equal-width reports retain 99.2% of oracle power. We give the power-optimal combining rule for given reports, and a rule using only their exactly known null distribution, valid under arbitrary dependence across hypotheses.

entry.title: Identification problem and quasi-maximum likelihood estimation for matrix-variate CP-factor models

link.title: Identification problem and quasi-maximum likelihood estimation for matrix-variate CP-factor models

entry.content: Matrix-valued time series, arising in diverse fields such as economics, neuroscience, and recommender systems, have become increasingly prominent in modern data analysis. Among various modeling frameworks, the matrix-variate CP-factor model represents an important and widely applicable class for capturing low-rank structures in matrix time series. In this paper, we provide a unified treatment for the identification problem of CP factor models using both analytic and algebraic tools. In particular, we characterize the parameter space as the union of two subspaces, one identifiable and the other non-identifiable. We show that existing estimation methods only apply to an open proper subset of the identifiable subspace. In contrast, we propose a quasi-maximum likelihood estimation (QMLE) procedure for CP factor models, which allows consistent estimation on the whole identifiable subspace. Moreover, we show that the estimated loading matrices by QMLE achieve a faster convergence rate compared to existing approaches. A simulation study and a real application are conducted to demonstrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed method.

entry.title: Streaming PCA: averaging from a geometric perspective

link.title: Streaming PCA: averaging from a geometric perspective

entry.content: We study principal component analysis (PCA) under memory constraints, a setting that is increasingly important in large-scale data analysis. Our focus is on Oja’s algorithm, which is a one-pass, memory-efficient algorithm requiring only $O(p)$ storage in the rank-one case and $O(pk)$ storage for $k$- PCA. The main goal is to develop a procedure based on Oja’s algorithm that is optimal without prior knowledge of the eigengap, which is otherwise needed to tune the learning rates effectively. We do this by first introducing a geometric perspective on the convergence of $k$-PCA: by embedding the Oja iterates into the exterior space, we establish an exact equivalence between $k$-PCA in the ambient space and $1$-PCA in the exterior space. This geometric viewpoint enables us to establish several convergence guarantees, including one based only on a single learning-rate schedule. Building on this geometric perspective, we develop an averaging theory for $k$-PCA and show that the resulting averaged estimator is adaptive: it achieves the nearly optimal convergence rate without prior knowledge of the eigengap. As an application, we construct memory-efficient estimators for elliptical component analysis (ECA) \cite{han2014scale,han2018eca}. Simulation studies and real data analysis are conducted to demonstrate the benefits of our proposed algorithms.

entry.title: OSCAR: Order-aware Sensitivity Correction for AI Rankings

link.title: OSCAR: Order-aware Sensitivity Correction for AI Rankings

entry.content: LLM judges evaluate candidate language models through pairwise comparisons of their responses. Judge-aware Bradley–Terry models aggregate pairwise comparisons by jointly estimating candidate scores and judge-specific sensitivities (how strongly each judge responds to quality differences), often interpreted as reliability. We show that this reading fails when judges prefer a display position. Even under balanced display orders or swap-and-average, omitting position attenuates fitted judge sensitivity by approximately the factor $1-D^2$ near equal quality, where $D$ is the judge’s net first-slot preference between equally good responses. We propose OSCAR, which jointly estimates candidate scores, judge sensitivities and judge-specific position, length and family effects, and provides confidence intervals for pairwise win probabilities that account for dependence within prompts. On held-out data, observed attenuation closely matches the prediction $1-D^2$ (correlation of log ratios 0.99). Across four datasets, position adjustment lowers held-out log loss by 14-23% and changes which judges would be dropped for low sensitivity on three datasets. On MT-Bench, it ranks GPT-4 first instead of claude-v1, matching human votes. Simulations with known parameters show improved recovery of judge sensitivities and candidate rankings, with 94.4-95.2% confidence interval coverage. Low estimated sensitivity alone is therefore not evidence of an unreliable judge.

entry.title: PICPIs: Prediction-Interval-Conditional Prediction Intervals

link.title: PICPIs: Prediction-Interval-Conditional Prediction Intervals

entry.content: A classical question in statistics is which observable quantities to condition on when drawing inferences about unobservable targets. For conformal prediction in nonparametric uncertainty quantification, standard marginal validity offers limited resolution at the prediction values on which decisions are based, and fully conditional guarantees with respect to the covariates are provably unattainable. We address this gap by introducing a prediction-based conditioning framework that we refer to as Prediction-Interval-Conditional Prediction Intervals (PICPIs). Formally, a PICPI is an interval $I$ satisfying a self-consistency condition: \(\mathbb{E} [Y \mid p(X) \in I] \in I,\) for predictive model $p$, contextual covariate $X$, and outcome $Y$. Thus, an interval simultaneously defines a stratum of prediction values and certifies that the mean outcome in that stratum lies in the same interval. This self-consistency condition yields data-adaptive strata without altering the original prediction. Such intervals can be constructed using practical algorithms. Under regularity of the prediction distribution, the constructed intervals cover all but an arbitrarily small fraction of prediction values and have widths that decrease at rate $n^{-1/3}$, up to logarithmic factors and the prediction error. Moreover, identifying these locally calibrated intervals can, in turn, inform downstream decision-making. We derive inference procedures for PICPIs in probabilistic prediction and multi-class classification, accompanied by theoretical guarantees. Empirical results are provided that compare PICPIs with existing interval-based baselines.

entry.title: GRACE: A General, Exact Changepoint Calculus

link.title: GRACE: A General, Exact Changepoint Calculus

entry.content: We introduce GRACE (the General Regime-Aware Changepoint Estimator), a general, globally exact multiple-changepoint detection and estimation framework in which arbitrary numbers of model parameters may change at or persist across estimated changepoint locations, and all permissible changepoint types and patterns of parameter sharing compete within a single $\ell_0$-penalized optimization. The analyst specifies which types of changepoints are permitted and which parameters each type must preserve, without specifying which changes actually occur, where they occur, or in what order. GRACE jointly estimates the number and locations of changepoints, the type of change at each location, the model fitted between changepoints, and all continuous parameters. As a direct consequence, GRACE can estimate models in which the slope persists across a mean shift. The generality of the framework is achieved through an exact dynamic-programming recursion that retains the accumulated fitting cost conditional on whichever parameters a subsequent change may preserve, tracking multiple parameters jointly when necessary. We establish the global exactness of the recursion and develop functional, penalty-based, and objective-bound pruning rules that eliminate candidates without sacrificing optimality. Ordinary optimal partitioning, FPOP, and CPOP are recovered as special cases, while piecewise-polynomial and seasonal models illustrate the broader range of permissible segment structures and transitions. The resulting framework supports heterogeneous changepoint types, parameter sharing across segments, and substantial parallel computation within a unified approach to exact changepoint estimation.

link.title: Heteroskedastic Canonical Polyadic Tensor Decomposition

entry.content: When minimizing the squared-error loss, the popular CP decomposition can be interpreted as parameter inference in a Gaussian model with a low-rank mean tensor and constant variance across the tensor entries. Our procedure is computationally competitive, with the same leading-order factor-update complexity as CP-ALS. We demonstrate HCP on synthetic experiments and an EEG application.

entry.title: Open-ended Scientific Discovery with Possibilistic Reasoning

link.title: Open-ended Scientific Discovery with Possibilistic Reasoning

entry.content: Autonomous scientific discovery with LLMs requires generating and testing hypotheses adaptively as evidence accumulates while maintaining statistical validity. Existing anytime-valid methods can handle data-dependent hypotheses, but open-ended discovery poses a deeper challenge: the best discovered hypothesis may still be the best of a bad lot, with better explanations yet undiscovered, while even background knowledge such as physical laws may require revision in light of new findings. In response, we formalize the problem as Abductive Autonomous Scientific Discovery (AASD) using possibility theory. We introduce abductive utility, a computable measure of discovery progress, and possibility frontier search, the first algorithm for AASD, which maintains anytime validity and achieves $\varepsilon$-optimal abductive utility asymptotically under suitable conditions. Experiments on synthetic and real-world scientific-discovery tasks show strong performance.

entry.title: Mean-Tilted Intervals: Regression and Dynamic Models

link.title: Mean-Tilted Intervals: Regression and Dynamic Models

entry.content: Mean-tilted intervals (MTIs) provide a fixed-content family of interval targets indexed by retained-mean balance. This paper develops generalized-Bayes computation for using those targets in regression and time-varying endpoint models after content and tilt have been specified. The update combines a prior with an exponentiated residual-product check loss, yielding uncertainty summaries for endpoint functions rather than a response-distribution model. A pseudo-asymmetric-Laplace normal-exponential representation gives generalized-inverse-Gaussian latent-scale updates and Gaussian conditional updates for one root when the other is fixed. The same representation gives deterministic ECM equations for generalized-posterior modes. We present ridge endpoint regression, a conditionally Gaussian shrinkage construction for the zero-tilt case, deterministic fixed-feature readouts, and dynamic linear endpoint states updated by alternating forward-filtering backward-sampling steps. entry.content: Modern experiments increasingly produce rich post-treatment objects—such as text, images, and video—that may provide early surrogate signals for outcomes that are delayed, expensive, or observed only for a subset of participants. Starting from pretrained surrogate embeddings, SIRNET learns a shared adapter jointly for outcome prediction, treatment propensity, and arm-specific surrogate marginalization, beyond the generic pretraining objective. The resulting covariate and surrogate representations provide a common interface for these nuisance tasks. The final treatment-effect estimate and confidence interval are obtained from cross-fitted orthogonal scores that attain the semiparametric efficiency bound under the stated nuisance-rate conditions. We also validate SIRNET’s performance in synthetic and semisynthetic experiments, as well as the Anti-Amyloid in Asymptomatic Alzheimer’s Disease (A4) trial, using frozen pretrained brain-MRI embeddings as surrogates for a long-term outcome.

entry.title: Dynamic Extended Generalized Many-Facet Rasch Model: A Unified Approach to Rater-Mediated Assessment

link.title: Dynamic Extended Generalized Many-Facet Rasch Model: A Unified Approach to Rater-Mediated Assessment

entry.content: Rating procedures are crucial in psychological and medical diagnosis, educational assessment, peer review, and grant evaluation. A major methodological challenge is disentangling multiple sources of variability in ratings, such as subject ability, rater behavior, and item characteristics. Item Response Theory-based models, most notably many-facet Rasch models and hierarchical rater models, have been widely adopted for jointly estimating subject, rater, and item effects, while retaining high interpretability. We introduce the Dynamic Extended Generalized Many-Facet Rasch model, a general class of Bayesian semiparametric models that integrate and extend existing approaches. Its measurement model allows location and discrimination parameters to depend jointly on item and rater characteristics and incorporates subject-item and rater-subject variation. The dynamic extension introduces a rater-specific cross-lagged effect capturing dependence on the previously rated subject, and a Bayesian P-spline capturing systematic changes in discrimination over the rating sequence, accounting for learning, fatigue, or adaptation effects. Subject heterogeneity is addressed through Bayesian nonparametric mixtures, flexibly learning the latent ability distribution without strict parametric assumptions and enabling model-based subject clustering. We also derive a closed-form, model-based inter-rater consensus coefficient and study its characteristics. We discuss theoretical properties, develop posterior computation strategies, and evaluate the model in simulation studies and two real-data applications.

entry.title: Changing Geographies of Violence in North and West Africa

link.title: Changing Geographies of Violence in North and West Africa

entry.content: This paper analyses spatial trends in armed conflicts in North and West Africa. It shows that all types of violence saw a significant increase in 2025. However, these violent incidents are distributed very unevenly across the region: while conflict is at its lowest in North Africa, the vast majority of violent incidents and victims are concentrated in five West African countries: Nigeria, Cameroon, Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger. Coastal countries are experiencing a very mixed picture: jihadism is not advancing as a front, from the Sahel toward the Gulf of Guinea, and most of the violence stems from local disputes, ethnic conflicts, and banditry. Second, the spatial indicator developed by the OECD/SWAC to track the evolution of this violence confirms that the conflict landscape is expanding at its margins and intensifying at its center. Even more concerning is that peripheral areas are increasingly being drawn directly into well-established conflict zones, rather than going through a gradual, low-intensity transition phase. The geography of expansion is shifting from a diffuse, low-intensity spread toward peripheral areas to a rapid outward expansion from dense, well-established conflict hotspots. The local indicator used in the report suggests that violence continues to spread to new locations at the margins of established conflict zones. At the heart of these zones, tensions are intensifying relative to their historical baseline levels, and a growing number of regions have experienced clashes for a decade or more. Projections indicate that the intensity of violence is expected to increase in 2026, reaching more than 15,000 incidents and more than 32,500 deaths. Much of the increase is explained by the growing number of conflicts in Nigeria. In the Sahel, fatalities should increase in Mali and decrease in Burkina Faso.

entry.title: cvxoptdes: convex optimal experiment design in R

link.title: cvxoptdes: convex optimal experiment design in R

entry.content: The cvxoptdes R-package provides a unified framework to perform convex optimal experiment design and online response optimization for linear, generalized linear and additive, nonlinear, and random intercept mixed models, using exclusively open-source solvers. It supports optimization and augmentation of weighted, penalized and convex constrained continuous designs across a discrete grid of candidate points and rounding to integer-valued designs using point-exchange algorithms or mixed-integer programming for orthogonally constrained designs, including the class of orthogonal minimally aliased response surface (OMARS) designs. Models and design constraints are defined and updated in an object-oriented context with the aim to facilitate the process of sequential (penalized) design augmentation analogous to online design procedures known from active learning and Bayesian optimization.

entry.title: De-biased Distribution Estimation for Locally Differential Private Survival Data

link.title: De-biased Distribution Estimation for Locally Differential Private Survival Data

entry.content: Sharing time-to-event data can leak sensitive information about individual participants in clinical studies. To protect the privacy of data, differential privacy (DP) framework offers rigorous protection for data sharing. The local variant of differential privacy is particularly appealing because each record is perturbed before it leaves the data owner or contributor. However, the injected perturbation distorts the true distribution of the source data, yielding low utility and invalid statistical inference with the released data. In this work, we propose a nonparametric estimator for the true survivor function via the deconvolution kernel function with locally differential private (LDP) right-censored survival data in which both the event times and the event indicators are privatized. Our estimator simultaneously de-biases the perturbation applied to the times and the errors induced by flipping the event indicators due to LDP. Theoretically, we establish the uniform consistency and point-wise asymptotic normality of the de-biased distribution estimator, and derive its uniform convergence rate together with the optimal bandwidth attaining that rate. Simulation studies and the analysis of a semi-synthetic dataset generated from the METABRIC breast cancer cohort demonstrate the performance of the proposed estimator across privacy budgets, censoring levels, and sample sizes. By the post-processing property of DP, the proposed de-biased estimator inherits the privacy guarantee while restoring valid inference on the survivor function.

entry.title: Sharp bounds for population and principal effects under latent sequential ignorability

link.title: Sharp bounds for population and principal effects under latent sequential ignorability

entry.content: Treatment decisions are often sequential and depend on information absent from the recorded history. Latent sequential ignorability models such assignment by assuming that baseline covariates and principal strata, defined by joint potential intermediate responses, account for confounding of later treatment. For two treatment periods with a binary intermediate response, we derive sharp population and principal effect bounds under a specified association between the potential responses and show that the two targets can require different optimizations to obtain sharp bounds. For population effects, optimization over latent treatment probabilities reduces to their feasible endpoints. Stronger selection between response types can be offset by making their outcome distributions more similar, preserving both the observed distribution and population marginal outcome distributions. This replacement can change effects within principal strata, whose sharp bounds may instead require interior treatment probabilities. Restrictions on differences in conditional effects can tighten the bounds without equating outcome levels. For binary outcomes, we give an exact finite algorithm that includes these interior assignments. We also develop inference under smoothness and estimation conditions. We illustrate the bounds in a study of gym attendance after an incentive program.

entry.title: Global Inference for High Dimensional Quantile Regression with Heterogeneity

link.title: Global Inference for High Dimensional Quantile Regression with Heterogeneity

entry.content: Quantile regression has received considerable attention in high dimensional methodology due to its robustness and ability to accommodate heteroskedasticity. Despite this attention, current inferential methods for high dimensional quantile regression have significant limitations—only testing significance, testing at a single quantile at a time, or assuming homoskedasticity. To generalize the inferences that can be drawn in high dimensional quantile regression, we introduce partial penalized Wald and rank score tests for testing linear hypotheses uniformly over a set of quantiles $\mathcal T$ under a heteroskedastic model. We propose globally adaptive local linear approximation (LLA) algorithms for folded concave penalized estimation and show that our global LLA algorithms recover ``testing oracles’’ for the full and reduced models with high probability. We then show that our global LLA estimators achieve the $\sqrt{s/n}$ oracle estimation rate uniformly over $\mathcal T$, establish Bahadur representations, and derive asymptotic distributions for the test statistics under the null and local alternatives. We develop a dual formulation incorporating adaptive penalty weights for the rank scores and use the strong oracle property to establish their oracle equivalence. Using empirical process techniques, we derive reference distributions based on suprema of squared Bessel processes, extending partial penalized inference beyond pointwise chi-square calibration.

entry.title: Decomposing the spectral density function of an ARMA process

link.title: Decomposing the spectral density function of an ARMA process

entry.content: Quasi-periodic oscillations are characterized by fitting Lorentzian functions to a nonparametric estimate of the power spectral density, a two-step procedure that separates estimation from modeling and does not accommodate measurement error. We develop a parametric alternative based on autoregressive moving-average (ARMA) processes observed with measurement error. We derive an exact decomposition of the ARMA spectral density into real-valued components, one for each class of autoregressive roots under complex conjugation, plus a polynomial term when the moving-average order is at least the autoregressive order. Each component is a Wrapped Cauchy kernel, and for complex roots it is accompanied by a conjugate-Poisson term that makes the peak asymmetric and displaces its maximum from the frequency given by the argument of the root. We obtain closed-form expressions for the location, height, width, and asymmetry of each peak, and a matching variance decomposition. Parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood through the Kalman filter, and all descriptors follow by plug-in. Simulations show that the closed-form peak location is recovered without appreciable bias. An X-ray binary light curve illustrates the methodology.

entry.title: The Quantification of Replicability

link.title: The Quantification of Replicability

entry.content: What does it mean to measure the replicability of scientific results? Is it merely determining whether results are consistent across studies? Much of the existing literature on replicability draws conclusions exclusively from the comparison of study results, in terms of observed estimates, uses a variety of different metrics, and ultimately collapses the comparison into a binary verdict of success or failure. This fails to differentiate between repeated errors and corroboration of the shared generative effect. We develop a unified Bayesian framework in which distinct but related notions of replicability are formally defined and jointly embedded within a single inferential structure. A single model answers four complementary questions: agreement among independent studies; consistency between the individual studies and the shared generative effect; agreement between an existing body of evidence and a new study from the same super-population; inference on the shared generative effect. In practice, we suggest quantifying replicability through posterior probabilities relative to regions of practical relevance. We illustrate these ideas in an eQTL (expression quantitative trait locus) analysis assessing the replicability of a regulatory effect across human ancestral groups.

link.title: Prior-Informed Generalizable Low-Rank Representation Learning via Regularized Adversarial Reweighting

entry.content: Modern learning problems increasingly leverage data from heterogeneous sources to improve robustness and generalizability under distribution shift, often with high-dimensional parameters admitting low-rank structure. Using Burer-Monteiro factorization, we optimize the nonconvex-concave objective by bifactored gradient descent with mirror ascent. We establish linear convergence to a statistical neighborhood of the population saddle point and derive an error bound that separates low-rank estimation from adversarial reweighting. We further show that PILLAR improves on vanilla group DRO when the latter’s excess conservativeness dominates source heterogeneity and prior misspecification. Simulations and an electronic health record study of suicide-attempt risk demonstrate improved worst-source and transported predictive accuracy.

entry.content: The Copula Active Subspaces (CAS) method of Part I estimates a non-Gaussian observation-noise density $\pi_{\boldsymbol{n}}$ from residual samples. Its KL divergence $\mathcal{D}{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi{\boldsymbol{n}}\,|\,\widehat\pi_{\boldsymbol{n}})$ admits an exact decomposition into marginal, projection and reduced-density terms and bounds the posterior KL divergence averaged over the true predictive distribution. We derive a priori bounds for these terms, together with estimates or bounds from residual samples. Weighted nearest-neighbour entropy estimates are used for the marginal and reduced-density terms, with asymptotic standard errors in exact rank coordinates. For the projection error, the score is fitted on one subsample, and its mean squared magnitude outside the retained subspace is estimated on the other. Corrections for score and rank-transform errors then give a theoretical upper bound with probability at least $1-\delta$. Tests on three known noise laws in dimension $d=20$ use the estimated rank transform. In $11$ of $12$ combinations of example and sample size, the sum of the two estimated terms and the trace bound exceeds the reference divergence after averaging over the estimated models. In these tests, score-estimation error is the largest contribution to looseness. The overestimate from the Gaussian log-Sobolev inequality alone is at most a factor of $1.98$.

entry.title: Identification and Estimation of Treatment Effects from Network Data with Confounded Social Links

link.title: Identification and Estimation of Treatment Effects from Network Data with Confounded Social Links

entry.content: In observational network data, the adoption of a treatment and the formation of social ties often depend on the same characteristics that affect outcomes. We propose a generalized propensity score for each unit’s effective treatment, built from a model for treatment assignment and a dyadic model for network formation, which may include latent node heterogeneity. The score is marginalized over the network given covariates rather than conditioned on the realized network, and the estimand is a population effect: the average effect of an exposure level for a unit drawn from the population of units and networks. We relate this estimand to those of methods that condition on the realized network and show what marginalizing costs and buys. It requires network formation to be unconfounded given observed covariates, a stronger assumption than unconfoundedness of treatment given the network. In exchange, it defines effects at exposure levels that poorly connected units cannot reach, and at levels every unit can reach it gives an estimator whose asymptotic variance is no larger than the network-conditional one. We combine the score with an augmented inverse probability weighting estimator, prove asymptotic normality as the number of networks grows with bounded network size, discuss what carries over to a single large sparse network, and apply the method to the effect of a political communication technology on political participation in Uganda.

entry.title: Cointegrated Regressors: Where Folded Concave Penalties Go Beyond LASSO

link.title: Cointegrated Regressors: Where Folded Concave Penalties Go Beyond LASSO

entry.content: LASSO is one of the most popular regularization methods for high-dimensional regression models. While cointegration is common in practical applications of predictive regressions with many regressors, the convex penalty of LASSO overly suppresses the coefficients of cointegrated regressors and therefore fails to deliver consistent parameter estimation. We employ folded concave penalties (FCP), including the well-known SCAD and MCP, to address this issue. Using FCP, we establish two asymptotic results: (i) a local oracle property for the penalized regression, and (ii) a global oracle property for regressions with a penalty-level constraint. In particular, the latter guarantees a global solution that consistently estimates the true coefficients and enjoys oracle prediction performance. Simulation studies and an application to predicting the euro area unemployment rate show that FCP improves variable selection and out-of-sample prediction relative to LASSO.

entry.title: Beyond the Damped Random Walk: Multiband AGN Variability from SDSS to Rubin LSST

link.title: Beyond the Damped Random Walk: Multiband AGN Variability from SDSS to Rubin LSST

entry.content: The flux variability of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs) is commonly modeled using the damped random walk (DRW), but increasingly rich multiband time-domain surveys motivate more flexible stochastic models that characterize variability beyond a single timescale and exploit dependence across bands. Multivariate continuous-time autoregressive moving average (MCARMA) processes extend the multivariate DRW to higher-order stochastic dynamics and provide a matrix-valued power spectral density for characterizing marginal variability and cross-band dependence. In a carefully selected Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Stripe~82 sample, higher-order models are selected for 109 of 134 AGNs (81.3\%), with substantial rather than marginal support in most objects; convergence diagnostics indicate that this fraction is conservative. The fitted models also reveal strong cross-band dependence that generally decreases with wavelength separation. Motivated by this richer structure, we investigate its recoverability under Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) observing conditions. Model-order recovery depends strongly on the underlying stochastic behavior as well as source brightness and observing cadence. Recovery is high across many of the simulated settings, but deteriorates when the characteristic features of higher-order variability become difficult to distinguish from the multivariate DRW. Additional simulations show that this loss of distinguishability can persist over a range of underlying variability behaviors. These results show that stochastic structure beyond the multivariate DRW is prevalent in our selected SDSS sample, while its recoverability with LSST depends on both observational conditions and the form of the underlying stochastic variability. The methodology is implemented in the Python package mcarma.

entry.title: Bayesian Uncertainty Quantification of Breast-Cancer Pathology AI Agreement under Reader- and Annotation-Condition-Dependent Reference Labels

link.title: Bayesian Uncertainty Quantification of Breast-Cancer Pathology AI Agreement under Reader- and Annotation-Condition-Dependent Reference Labels

entry.content: Human reference labels used to evaluate medical AI can vary across readers and annotation workflows. We quantified agreement of a fixed pathology AI system with a future qualified reader without treating inferred consensus as error-free biological truth. Linked Evaluation and Unbiased NuCLS multirater data were analyzed using a fixed external HoVer-Net decision vector. The selected frame contained 1,144 anchors, 52 fields of view, five slides/patients, and five primary readers. The target was fixed-AI agreement with a future reader, with descriptive contrast $\Delta=\theta_E-\theta_U$. Analyses included raw agreement and iMRMC benchmarks, reader-only and shared-detectability Bayesian models, structural sensitivities, adversarial simulations, and predictive assessment. Among 5,188 reader-anchor pairs observed in both conditions, 19.62% changed AI-agreement state, while raw agreement was 0.5466 in Unbiased and 0.5473 in Evaluation. The reader-only model gave $\Delta=-0.0008$ (95% CrI, $-0.0033$ to $0.0008$), and the shared-detectability model gave $\Delta\approx0$ ($-0.0140$ to $0.0127$). Across structural perturbations, absolute agreement ranged from 0.420 to 0.646 in Unbiased and 0.409 to 0.640 in Evaluation. Frozen adversarial simulations met the comparative-stability criterion (median $R=0.295$; 14/16 model-scenario cells had $R<1$). Held-out-AI prediction supported shared predictive information, but varied by slide composition. The Evaluation-minus-Unbiased contrast was comparatively stable, whereas absolute agreement was structurally sensitive. These findings do not establish equivalence, causal assistance effects, biological accuracy, or new-patient transportability. Evaluations using variable human references should report reader population, selected frame, observation mechanism, and structural sensitivity.

entry.title: The price of a weak shadow variable: inference under nonignorable missingness as relevance vanishes

link.title: The price of a weak shadow variable: inference under nonignorable missingness as relevance vanishes

entry.content: When an outcome is missing not at random, identification is commonly restored by a shadow variable: a covariate that predicts the outcome but is excluded from the response mechanism. The literature treats the first requirement, relevance, as a yes-or-no condition. We make it continuous, parametrizing it by a scalar that scales the shadow variable’s entire contribution to the moment conditions, and ask what inference costs as that scalar vanishes. One functional of the inverse weight governs the answer. We characterize it exactly, show that it fixes the effective sample size, and use it to sharpen the rates of the estimator that avoids the weight. The characterization is concrete. Whether the functional saturates or diverges turns not on boundedness of the outcome but on whether the tilting variable has an atom at its essential supremum: a binary outcome saturates, a uniform one does not. It also bounds how far a scanned set reaches, and that reach grows only as the square root of the logarithm of the sample size, so a thousandfold increase buys one unit of tilt while the set to be scanned widens without limit.

entry.title: An Unscented PrO Kalman Filter

link.title: An Unscented PrO Kalman Filter

entry.content: Predictively-oriented (PrO) filtering for state-space models was proposed in Shen et al. [2026] as a promising route to avoiding over-confident inferences in settings where either the dynamical model, the measurement model, or both, could be misspecified. Our focus is on nonlinear state-space models, where the local linearisation used to construct the PrO filter in Shen et al. [2026] deteriorates as nonlinearities enter either the dynamical model or the measurement model. Our proposed solution is based on unscented transforms, an established tool from classical filtering which provides a more accurate mechanism to propagate Gaussian uncertainty through a nonlinear functional, and which includes the cubature rule as a special case. We introduce two variants: replacing the linearisation in the predict step alone, which we call UKF-PrO, has a computational cost comparable to the existing PrO filter; replacing it in the update step as well, UKF-PrO+, requires a substantially more expensive joint optimisation. Performance is empirically assessed on the Lorenz96 model under conditions of increasing difficulty, in which the state-space model is systematically misspecified; we find that UKF-PrO with the parameters of the cubature Kalman filter offers consistent improvements, which become substantial under strong nonlinearity, whereas the default unscented parameters are unreliable, and that the full update-step extension with the same parameters does not justify its additional cost.

entry.title: Comparing randomized trials

link.title: Comparing randomized trials

entry.content: Disagreements between randomized trials that address the same causal question pose challenges for the interpretation and synthesis of evidence. We sketch a causal framework for comparing the results of randomized trials that explicitly accommodates the possibility of trial engagement effects. Using counterfactual outcomes defined under joint interventions on treatment assignment and trial-related actions, we compare trial-native treatment effects with the effects transported from one trial to the population of another in a common target population. We show that standard conditions for transporting treatment effects across trial populations are not sufficient to guarantee agreement between transported and trial-native effects. Agreement additionally requires conditions governing how trial-related actions affect outcome across studies - for example, absence of trial engagement effects, equivalence of such effects across trials, or lack of interaction between trial engagement and treatment assignment. Our framework clarifies potential sources of disagreement across trials and extends existing approaches to study comparison to settings in which trial engagement effects may be present.

entry.title: Probable but Not Valid: A Psychometric Audit of Decision Models as Synthetic Survey Respondents

link.title: Probable but Not Valid: A Psychometric Audit of Decision Models as Synthetic Survey Respondents

entry.content: Language models are increasingly used to create synthetic survey samples, also called silicon samples. Decision models are a new class of language models that return a probability for each point of a rating scale instead of text. We ask whether these models, or the newest generative LLMs, can stand in for human respondents on a psychometric survey. We test fourteen decision models from eleven providers and 47 generative LLMs on an open Lithuanian organisational-psychology survey (n=263, 68 items), with 100 real respondent profiles, the Psychometric Similarity Score (PSS) and statistical baselines. The best generative model, MiniMax M3, reaches PSS 0.813. This is level with a Gaussian copula fit only on other respondents (0.824) and below a copula fit in sample (0.927). A second sample of 100 real people scores below the best models, so at this size PSS cannot rank them against real respondents. In 5 of 10 product lines the newest generative release scores below an earlier release of the same line beyond resampling noise, and none gains beyond it. With the default rounded readout, 13 of 14 decision models score below the generative reference gpt-5.4-mini. Of the 47 generative models, 33 reproduce the pattern of item correlations better than any decision model. Averaged over respondents, the probability vectors are much closer to the human item marginals than rounded answers. They also rank respondents about as well as a profile regression fit on 163 real people. As forecasts of each person’s own answers, however, every decision model is worse than the answer frequencies of other respondents, mainly because its average vector differs from them. The profile regression improves on these frequencies by only 1.0%, so the profile fields say little about how a person answers. Synthetic respondents built on such profiles should therefore aim at sample-level fidelity.

entry.title: An Algebraic Approach to Constrained K-means Clustering

link.title: An Algebraic Approach to Constrained K-means Clustering

entry.content: Clustering is typically performed using only object features, although additional information about relationships between objects may be available and can be incorporated through constraints. Among these, pairwise constraints require two objects to belong to the same cluster or to different clusters. Several extensions of the k-means algorithm accommodate such constraints, but they sometimes fail to find a feasible assignment or incur high computational cost. Motivated by these limitations, we propose an algebraic approach to k-means clustering with pairwise constraints. The algorithm simplifies the constraints using Gr"{o}bner bases before optimization, improving the efficiency of cluster assignment. It can also detect whether the constraint set has a feasible assignment before optimization. Comparative experiments with existing algorithms showed that the proposed algorithm achieved comparable or better clustering quality at a lower computational cost, particularly when the numbers of constraints and clusters were small.

entry.title: Bayesian adaptive design for neural recruitment curves

link.title: Bayesian adaptive design for neural recruitment curves

entry.content: Nonlinear response models remain ubiquitous across disciplines with recruitment curves describing muscle response to neural stimulation. Conventional acquisition methods typically rely on static uniform sampling, requiring many stimuli, while adaptive threshold-hunting designs such as ML-PEST forfeit accurate characterization of the overall curve. We present a Bayesian adaptive design that uses posterior uncertainty over curve parameters to propose stimuli that maximize information gain across the full recruitment curve. We additionally implement a focused acquisition method that can target arbitrary subset of curve parameters, which we use to evaluate and interpret our design. In simulations, our design outperforms uniform sampling in recovering threshold while matching ML-PEST, and outperforms ML-PEST in predictive curve accuracy while matching uniform. It likewise matches our threshold-focused acquisition, suggesting our design doesn’t trade off threshold estimation for recovering the curve. We further show data collected using our design yields greater power when detecting a change in threshold in intervention studies. Our design proposes the next stimulus within 5 seconds, making it feasible for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) experiments. Finally, we validate our design in TMS experiments and provide a library for Python, called onMEP, for online acquisition of neural recruitment curves.

entry.title: Recurrent Barycenter Encoder: Prediction, Simulation and Applications to Time Series Analysis

link.title: Recurrent Barycenter Encoder: Prediction, Simulation and Applications to Time Series Analysis

entry.content: This dissertation has two parts. In the first part we theoretically develop a framework that extends the optimal transport barycenter problem from independent data with observed covariates to processes whose relevant covariate is their own history. Given a stationary stochastic process, our framework shows there exists an invertible transport map that extracts from it an iid component whose distribution is the barycenter of the conditional distributions of the input process on its own past. This extracted iid sequence thus captures the innovation or noise component of the process that is not explained by the process’s own past. In the second part of this thesis we implement an effective algorithm to solve this problem and test it against synthetic data generated with some well-known models in time series analysis for which the solution is known in closed-form. We then show how this method can be applied to build a predictive sampler for such processes, and assess the accuracy of this predictive sampler both with the aforementioned synthetic data and with real-world time series such as the S&P 500 and Bitcoin 4-hour returns, and the daily records of the North Atlantic Oscillation index from the NOAA Physical Sciences Laboratory. Finally, we demonstrate an application of the sampler to path simulation with a well-known time series model.

entry.title: Rate-Based Causal Discovery for Heavy-Tailed Models

link.title: Rate-Based Causal Discovery for Heavy-Tailed Models

entry.content: In many complex systems, such as river networks and financial markets, extreme events propagate from causes to their effects, and the largest observations carry the most information about the underlying causal structure. Existing methods for causal discovery in extremes, however, are tailored to specific mechanisms, such as linear or max-linear models. This work develops causal discovery for heavy-tailed homogeneous structural causal models, a flexible class that contains linear, max-linear and norm-type mechanisms, which may differ from node to node. In these models, the causal structure is encoded by ancestral impulse responses, which measure how a shock at one node is transmitted to its descendants. We propose the extremal minimum ratio estimator of these responses, which uses only observations in which the potential cause is extreme. The estimator is consistent under regular variation alone, and we derive its exact rates of convergence and limiting distributions, which depend on both the causal relation and the type of mechanism. Building on these rates, we construct consistent estimators of the causal order and of the full set of ancestral relations, using a threshold that adapts to the data and requires no knowledge of the tail index. The method is illustrated on simulated data and on river discharges in the upper Danube basin.

entry.title: A model-assisted design for phase I oncology drug combination trials incorporating backfill

link.title: A model-assisted design for phase I oncology drug combination trials incorporating backfill

entry.content: Historically, phase I oncology trials were designed with the focus to find the highest tolerable dose. However, given the FDA’s acknowledgment that the highest tolerable dose might not be the dose which is optimal biologically, there is an increased emphasis the development of designs that explore the dose-toxicity and dose-efficacy relationship. Backfill designs have emerged as a popular response to address this need by allocating participants to doses deemed safe while awaiting participants outcomes. Previous designs have explored how to assign participants to doses in backfill designs in a rigorous manner while providing simplicity and performance (a class of designs known as model-assisted) for single agents. Still, a research gap exists in the lack of model-assisted backfill designs for drug combinations. Frequently, the combinations two of cancer agents are explored in phase I trials, with the goal of identifying the highest tolerable combination. This paper incorporates and extends methodology based on previous model-assisted backfill designs to provide clinicians with a simple-to-use backfill design for phase I drug combination trials.

entry.title: Energy-Guided Learning for Heat Equation with Noisy Source: Optimal Estimation and Generalization Bounds

link.title: Energy-Guided Learning for Heat Equation with Noisy Source: Optimal Estimation and Generalization Bounds

entry.content: Data and the governing partial differential equations (PDEs) of continuous-time dynamical systems provide rich structure for statistical learning. A central challenge is how to integrate data with PDE constraints in a principled way to improve generalization. In this paper, we characterize the statistical estimation and generalization properties of learning solutions to the heat equation with a noisy source function from finite, randomly sampled data. We first derive a novel variational formulation, which we characterize as the minimizer of loss function for an energy regularized and ellipticity debiased Sobolev regression. By formulating the learning task as a supervised problem over space-time domains under physically meaningful norms, our approach goes beyond the traditional supervised learning framework by effectively leveraging \emph{auxiliary data}—samples of the source function of the heat equation—to design a \emph{physics-informed energy regularization}. Our analysis reveals that learning in linear parabolic PDEs exhibits intrinsic anisotropy between spatial and temporal regularity, in sharp contrast to the static elliptic problems, leading to fundamentally different estimation and generalization behaviors. Specifically, we derive non-asymptotically rate-optimal estimation errors, as well as generalization error, which explicitly capture the interplay among temporal sampling, spatial resolution, and solution smoothness. Our numerical experiments demonstrate substantial orders of magnitude of reduction in testing errors against various physics-informed neural network methods on various parabolic and hyperbolic PDEs.

By formulating the learning task as a supervised problem over space-time domains under physically meaningful norms, our approach goes beyond the traditional supervised learning framework by effectively leveraging \emph{auxiliary data}—samples of the source function of the heat equation—to design a \emph{physics-informed energy regularization}. Our analysis reveals that learning in linear parabolic PDEs exhibits intrinsic anisotropy between spatial and temporal regularity, in sharp contrast to the static elliptic problems, leading to fundamentally different estimation and generalization behaviors. Specifically, we derive non-asymptotically rate-optimal estimation errors, as well as generalization error, which explicitly capture the interplay among temporal sampling, spatial resolution, and solution smoothness. Our numerical experiments demonstrate substantial orders of magnitude of reduction in testing errors against various physics-informed neural network methods on various parabolic and hyperbolic PDEs.

entry.title: A Cosine-Projection Framework for Choosing Among Cox HR, D-RMST, and Average-Hazard Tests in Survival Trials

link.title: A Cosine-Projection Framework for Choosing Among Cox HR, D-RMST, and Average-Hazard Tests in Survival Trials

entry.content: The log-rank/Cox hazard-ratio test remains the standard approach for the primary analysis of randomized trials with time-to-event endpoints and is fully efficient under proportional hazards (PH). Two model-free alternatives that have recently gained attention are the difference in restricted mean survival time (D-RMST), a contrast on the time scale, and the more recently proposed ratio of average hazards (RAH), a contrast on the rate scale. Simulation studies suggest that the RAH-based test can outperform both under delayed treatment effects, but its efficiency has not been characterized analytically, and no unified framework explains how censoring and accrual affect the efficiency ordering among these tests. We show that all three statistics share a weighted-log-rank representation and derive their asymptotic relative efficiencies under local alternatives, including the first analytic efficiency results for the RAH-based test. Geometrically, each test defines a direction in a function space and the anticipated treatment effect defines a signal direction. A test’s efficiency relative to the oracle test equals the squared cosine of the angle between these directions, so the asymptotic relative efficiency of any two tests is a ratio of squared cosines. Because censoring and accrual enter through an information weight, the framework shows how design choices can alter, and even reverse, the efficiency ordering. We illustrate the framework using the CheckMate 057 immunotherapy trial and corroborate the theoretical results through simulations spanning proportional- and non-proportional-hazards settings.

entry.title: Closed forms all the way up: the sample variance of four observations

link.title: Closed forms all the way up: the sample variance of four observations

entry.content: The distribution function $F(y)=\Pr(S^2\le y)$ of the sample variance $S^2$ of four independent observations is elementary on its entire support for every polynomial parent density on $[0,1]$ (without loss of generality), and we give it in finite closed form for the uniform, Beta$(2,1)$ and Beta$(2,2)$ parents. The support splits at $y = 1/6$, $2/9$ and $1/4$, with the ceiling at $1/3$, all fixed by geometry: in coordinates aligned with the cube diagonal the event $S^2\le y$ is a ball of radius $\sqrt{3y}$, the cube projects to a rhombic dodecahedron, and these are the levels at which the ball reaches its faces, edges and two kinds of vertices. The divergence theorem reduces every moment of the clipped ball to integrals along circular arcs, so each regime closes in algebraic functions of $\sqrt{y}$ and inverse trigonometric functions. For the uniform parent the only non-obvious constant is $K_g = 12\sqrt2\arctan\sqrt2$, proportional to the mean width of the cuboctahedron; the Beta constants are rational expressions in $\pi$, $\sqrt2$, $\sqrt3$ and $\arctan\sqrt2$, as in the uniform case. At $n = 4$ the normal-theory $\chi^2$ recipe used in acceptance testing misplaces the $99$th percentile of $S^2$ by $50\%$ for the uniform parent. For three observations, polynomial parents also give elementary closed forms (arXiv:2609.25333), but two elementary cases in a row do not guarantee a third, and we make no claim beyond $n = 4$.

entry.title: Precision follows the decision: how well an acceptance probability is known for mean-spread release rules

link.title: Precision follows the decision: how well an acceptance probability is known for mean-spread release rules

entry.content: Many release rules accept a lot when a statistic built from the sample mean and standard deviation stays within a limit, and the probability that a process passes such a rule can be computed exactly for a broad class of parent distributions. This paper asks how well that probability is itself known once the parent has been estimated. Under a stated reference posterior the answer is an interval, narrow where a lot clearly passes or fails and wide where it is contested. In ninety-eight published content-uniformity lots that position, not the sample size, sets the width: among the forty-eight lots assayed at the same ten units, and so equally informed about the spread, the $95\%$ interval runs from essentially zero width to $0.96$. With the operating point held fixed while test and estimation sample grow together, the interval narrows only slowly, the contraction of the posterior being offset by the steepening of the operating characteristic; a calibrated study at the sample sizes of $1207$ occupational exposure assessments shows the same under a half-plane rule. For a pure-spread rule under a Normal parent the interval has an exact chi-square form in the plug-in value and the two sample sizes, extending to the mean-spread wedge with a measured residual and containing Bergum’s lower bound as one endpoint. With the parent’s posterior formed from the same published summaries through the evaluator’s own likelihood, the qualitative pattern survives but shape moves both endpoints and width: on the same lots a strong right skew lowers the pessimistic endpoint by up to a fifth and widens the interval by up to $0.22$. At the content-uniformity operating point studied, under a Normal parent, the symmetric error bar in standard use puts the lower endpoint $0.21$ too high and returns an upper endpoint above one, even with the full posterior covariance.

entry.title: Stable Causal Estimation with Optimal Transport

link.title: Stable Causal Estimation with Optimal Transport

entry.content: In observational studies, the overlap assumption, also called positivity, is frequently strained in practice. Limited overlap destabilizes widely used estimators such as inverse propensity weighting (IPW), whose variance depends on density ratios that explode as propensity scores approach zero or one. To address this challenge, we propose the Stable Transport Estimator (STE), an optimal transport-based approach for estimating average causal effects when overlap holds but strict overlap fails. Unlike IPW, the variance of STE contains no density-ratio factor; it is governed by the transport map itself and stays finite under bounded moments, even when density ratios diverge. By replacing reweighting with a geometry-aware transport map, STE constructs stable counterfactual comparisons without requiring density estimation or propensity score modeling. STE further extends to settings where the overlap condition is violated: when covariate supports overlap only partially, a linear interpolation transport map enables principled extrapolation with explicit bias-variance trade-offs. We establish consistency, asymptotic normality, and a variance characterization that makes explicit the contribution of the estimated transport map to the asymptotic variance. Across synthetic and real datasets, STE demonstrates improved robustness, reduced bias, and markedly more stable variance compared to existing estimators.

entry.title: Moment-Calibrated Conformal Prediction with Side Information

link.title: Moment-Calibrated Conformal Prediction with Side Information

entry.content: For a fixed conformal score function, standard split conformal prediction calibrates a prediction set using the empirical distribution of the conformal scores, without using available side information about the data. We propose a moment-calibrated approach that uses such information to reduce variability across calibration data sets. Side information involving the covariates, the response, or both is expressed as moment restrictions, which are enforced through empirical likelihood weights on the calibration data points. The resulting weighted empirical distribution of the scores determines the weighted empirical quantile without changing the score function. We establish finite-sample bounds on training-conditional and marginal coverage of the moment-calibrated prediction set. We derive asymptotic distributions for training-conditional coverage and average prediction-set size, show that their asymptotic variances are no larger than the corresponding variances under standard split conformal prediction, and characterize when the reductions are strict. In the semi-supervised setting, we identify an optimal moment function of a given covariate representation, develop implementations using prespecified moment functions or a function learned by cross-fitting, and quantify the effect of the unlabeled sample size. We also extend the method to coverage conditions indexed by a class of functions of the covariates through weighted quantile regression. Numerical studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.
